1.why: The recovery record stores no user or email identifier, and /api/verify only checks token existence, expiry, and single-use status.

2.why: A reset token is a bearer value with no user binding, so an unused code can be verified by any other session.

3.why: Password reset changes only the current session state and global password hash; other stored sessions are not invalidated.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with TLS certificates and HTTP redirects to HTTPS, but the code does not specify or verify the latest TLS version.

5.why: TLS protects transport and passwords are Argon2-hashed, but reset tokens are kept in memory and exposed in JSON/logs rather than encrypted.

6.why: The user-facing recovery message is generic, but the simulated delivery reveals the reset token in page logs rather than guarding it.

7.why: Server-side length/format validation is applied to email, token, password, and MFA input, and client messages are written with textContent rather than unescaped HTML.

8.why: The only redirect is a fixed HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect to localhost, preventing open redirects, although a hospital domain is not explicitly shown.

9.why: No email templating is present, and the simulated delivery output is plain text without user-supplied HTML or scripts.

10.why: Generic error responses avoid leaks, but the page and console logs print the reset token and MFA code.

11.why: Passwords are hashed with Argon2id, but the MFA code 482916 is hardcoded in the source, so secret codes are not kept out of the code.

12.why: No default username/password is present, but the fixed MFA code acts as a known default secret in the flow.

13.why: Recovery, token verification, and MFA attempts are limited by IP/session counters and block after repeated failures.

14.why: The recovery endpoint returns the same generic message for any syntactically valid email and performs no account existence lookup.

15.why: Reset tokens are cryptographically random 64-character hex values, but they are not bound to the requesting user.
